results.summary: This project implements an 8-bit pseudo-random number generator based on the Xorshift algorithm. It accepts an 8-bit seed on the input pins and, after a two-cycle latency, produces a new pseudo-random 8-bit value on the output pins every clock cycle. The design is purely digital and requires no external hardware; it can be tested by applying a seed and observing the output sequence. Silicon tests confirm that it works as intended, with the same seed always producing the same first random output.

This is a baremetal RISC-V RV32E system-on-chip that includes a UART, a QSPI memory controller for PSRAM and flash, a generic SPI interface, and a sigma-delta audio emulator. It is designed to run firmware from external NOR flash and requires a PMOD with flash and PSRAM for operation. The design was tested by the author and successfully ran MicroPython for RV32E and played audio. It is notable for being a compact RISC-V SoC implementation on a Tiny Tapeout tile.

This analog block implements the fine-resolution part of a time-to-digital converter using time interpolation. It converts an input pulse of 20 to 60 nanoseconds into a periodic square wave with a period 90 times longer, allowing a low-frequency counter to measure the pulse width with high resolution. The circuit requires external hardware including a signal generator, a 13uA current source, and an oscilloscope for testing. It is a transistor-level analog design intended for applications such as digital communications, radar, and particle physics.

This design is a linear feedback shift register random number generator that interfaces via a Wishbone bus to fit within the Tiny Tapeout pin constraints. It allows loading a seed through the bus and then outputs a pseudo-random bit stream. Testing requires a cocotb testbench and a microcontroller on the development board to apply the correct startup signals. The design is a compact digital implementation of an LFSR with bus interface.

This is an 8-bit microcontroller system-on-chip called LISA, featuring a Tiny Tapeout Logic Controller and multiple communication interfaces including SPI, UART, and I2C. It is supported by a custom C-based assembler, linker, and a Python-based debugger for programming and debugging. The design requires external SPI flash and SRAM for program storage and data memory. The toolchain is partially functional, with the C compiler still under development and lacking floating-point support.

This project implements a ring-oscillator-based physically unclonable function (PUF) with 8 bits of challenge-response pairs. It uses 32 ring oscillators per bit, selected by the challenge, and races counters to produce a response bit. The design requires no external hardware and is tested by applying challenges and observing responses, though responses may vary with temperature. The author seeks collaboration to characterize the PUF's uniqueness, reliability, and entropy across many devices.

This is an implementation of a simple 8-bit SUBNEG CPU that requires external parallel SRAM for program and data storage. It provides control signals for interfacing with external SRAM and latches, and the program must be loaded into SRAM by an external device before enabling the CPU. The design outputs internal state bits for debugging and requires additional hardware such as a 3.3V SRAM, address latch, and output latch. It is a minimal CPU design intended for educational or experimental use.

This project generates GPS intermediate frequency signals with configurable parameters including satellite ID, code phase, Doppler shift, and SNR. It includes a register bank configurable via UART and a core with a Gold code generator, NCO, and PRNGs for noise generation. The design outputs sine and cosine signals with and without noise, and can be used to test GPS receiver search algorithms. External hardware such as a microprocessor or FPGA can be used to provide the navigation message input.

This accelerator calculates the Mandelbrot set iteration z = z^2 + c using 32-bit IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic, performing one iteration per clock cycle. It accepts the complex number c via a shift register interface and outputs the iteration count and an unbounded flag when the result exceeds the bound. The design requires no external hardware and was tested by generating a 256x256 image of the Mandelbrot set, taking about 24 minutes when manually clocked. It is notable for implementing floating-point arithmetic in a compact hardware design.

This project implements four NIST statistical tests (Frequency, Block Frequency, Runs, and Longest Run of Ones) to evaluate random bit sequences. It also includes an analog LFSR with configurable delay lines that can act as a conventional LFSR, oscillator, or chaotic oscillator. The design accepts random bits as input and outputs test results, and requires external hardware for configuration and monitoring. It is based on published works on low-cost on-chip randomness tests.
